chapter: New York, the Lafayette and the Cotton Club
title: Bill Robinson as a tap dancer and the double standard
summary: Crawford calls Bill Robinson the greatest tap dancer, better than Astaire, and comments that Black performers only recently gained wider opportunity.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Oh, now, right, now I see. So that's when -- and you say Bill Robinson was working with the band, that he was working the club.
No. Bill Robinson was the featured star when we were on the road in some theater. That's when he --

Oh. You know, a guy told me a story once. He told me -- let me see. He was -- that you all were working here, that you all -- sometime in the '30s, working with Bill Robinson, and Robinson was dancing out in the audience or something, and he did --
Well, he worked with -- Bill Robinson was a featured star. We worked with Billy Bill about three times off and on. We'd get him grouped moved together, Bill Robinson, he loved us.
Now, oh -- yeah, he liked you a lot, but you didn't like him because of the --
What did you think of him as a dancer?
Oh, at that time the greatest tap dancer in the world. That includes Fred Astaire, all the rest of them.
You know, so you don't think Fred Astaire was as good a tap dancer as Bill Robinson?
No. He was good, but not good as Bill Robinson, up and down the stairs and creative. That man was something else.
That -- like at the time what did -- did the musicians talk?
Alone, I'll have me a cup of coffee, sweetheart, when you get time.

At that time did -- did the musicians -- what did the musicians think about like what they later called -- they may have called it the same thing, like a double standard, you know, like how you could have somebody like Bill Robinson, who was the greatest tap dancer in the world, but seeing somebody like Fred Astaire would get the movies and the -- did musicians talk much about those kind of things?
Well, I'm pretty sure -- I'm pretty

sure you understand that. Just recently did the Black man get his feet into anything. He had the surface -- the surface, playing around the world, we used to call it. Black theater, even white would come, but up until Jackie Robinson, Roy Campanella, et cetera, moved in and (inaudible) got their feet --
